Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 62, verse 1:

Surat al-Jumu'ah (Sura of the Congregation)

It is Madani (Medinan), as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn Yasar said: it is Makki (Meccan), and this is also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The first view is the correct one, because of what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and others from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We were sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when the Surah of al-Jumu'ah was revealed," the hadith to its end, which will come shortly, God willing. Its (the surah's) revelation after the Hijrah by some time is agreed upon. Also, the matter of the dispersal (al-infidad) contained at the end of the surah, and likewise the matter of the Jews indicated by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Say: O you who have become Jews, if you claim﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 6], etc., did not occur except in Medina. Its verses are eleven, without disagreement.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that when He, exalted be He, mentioned earlier the condition of Musa, peace be upon him, with his people and their harm to him, censuring them for that, He mentioned in this surah the condition of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the excellence of his community, honouring them, so that the excellence between the two communities may be seen. For this reason it touches upon mention of the Jews. Also, when there was related there the words of 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿and giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6], He, glory be to Him, said here: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a Messenger from among them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2], indicating that he is the one of whom 'Isa gave good tidings. Also, when He concluded that surah with the command to jihad and called it ﴿a trade﴾ [al-Saff: 10], He concluded this one with the command to the Friday congregation and informed that this is better than worldly trade. Also, in both surahs there is an indication of lining up in worship: in the first it is evident, and in this one because it contains the command to the Friday prayer, which requires the congregation, which entails lining up, among other things. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite in the Friday prayer, with its surah, and ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], as Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Jabir ibn Samurah that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite in the Maghrib prayer on Friday night ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1] and ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1], and he used to recite in the last 'Isha' prayer on Friday night the Surah of al-Jumu'ah and al-Munafiqun." In that is an indication of the increased excellence of this surah.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth glorifies God﴾, a renewed glorification in the manner of continuity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 62, verse 2:

﴿He it is who sent among the unlettered (ummiyyin) a messenger from among themselves﴾ Glorified is He; by "the unlettered" He means the Arabs, because most of them neither write nor read.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i have related from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not calculate." By this is meant that they remain upon the original state of their mothers' birth: they have not learned writing and calculation, so they are upon their first natural disposition. Thus "ummi" is a relative term derived from "umm" (mother), the mother who bore him. It has also been said that it is a relative term to the "umma" of the Arabs, and it has been said that it refers to Umm al-Qura (Mecca). The first (view) is the most well known. Some commentators, in explaining it, restricted themselves to saying that it means one who does not write. As for writing, it is said that it began in al-Ta'if, whose people took it from the people of al-Hira, who were from the people of al-Anbar. The word "al-Amin" has been read with the omission of the relative ya' (i.e., "al-Ummi" becomes "al-Umm" in the reading attributed to some). ﴿a messenger from among themselves﴾, that is, existing from among their number. So "min" is partitive. The partitive sense may be either with regard to the genus, in which case it does not indicate that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was unlettered; or with regard to the particular quality shared by most of them, in which case it does indicate it. A group of scholars chose this (second) view. So the meaning is: a messenger from among them, unlettered like them. ﴿who recites to them His verses﴾, despite his being unlettered like them, from whom no reading or learning was known. ﴿and purifies them﴾ is coordinated with "yatlu" and so is also an attribute of "rasulan"; that is, he brings them to that by which they become purified and pure from the filth of beliefs and deeds.

﴿and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom﴾ is also an attribute of "rasulan", arranged in existence after the recitation. The purification, which is an expression for perfecting the soul according to its practical faculty and refining it as a branch of its perfection according to the theoretical faculty, which is attained through learning that follows recitation, was placed between them only to signify that each of the ordered matters is a great blessing in its own right, deserving gratitude. Had the order of existence been observed, it might have come to mind that the whole is one single blessing, as passed in Surat al-Baqara. This is the secret in expressing the Qur'an sometimes as "verses" and at other times as "the Book and the Wisdom", as a symbol that, by consideration of each title, it is a separate blessing. It is not harmed by the inclusion of "Wisdom" of the rulings and laws found within the prophetic traditions, as stated by some of the eminent scholars. It has also been permitted that "the Book and the Wisdom" be a metonymy for all transmitted and rational sciences, like the heavens and the earth with all existents, and the Ansar and the Muhajirun with all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It contains, regarding the greatness of his knowledge (ﷺ), what it contains, and even if he had no other sign than that, it would suffice, as al-Busiri indicated with his saying:

"Your knowledge in the unlettered is sufficient as a miracle, in the Age of Ignorance, and his upbringing in orphanhood."

* * *

﴿And indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ from polytheism and the corruption of the Age of Ignorance. This is an explanation of the intensity of their need for one who would guide them, although the attribution of error to them is in terms of the majority, since among them was one guided, such as Waraqa and his like. In the statement there is a removal of what might be suspected from his (ﷺ) having learned from others. "Wa-in" is the lightened (mukhaffafa) form, and the "lam" is the distinguishing lam (lam al-fariqa).

﴿Wa-akharina﴾ is the plural of ﴿akhar﴾, meaning "others." It is coordinated with ﴿al-ummiyyin﴾, so the sense is "and among others ﴿minhum﴾," that is, among the unlettered (ummiyyin). The ﴿min﴾ here is for specification (li-l-tabyin). ﴿Lamma yalhaqu bihim wa-huwa al-'Aziz al-Hakim﴾ means that they have not yet joined them, but they will join them. These are the people who came after the Companions until the Day of Religion (yawm al-din).

It is also permissible that it be coordinated with the object in ﴿wa-yu'allimuhum﴾, so that the meaning is "and He teaches them and teaches others." When teaching continues until the end of time, all of it is ascribed to its first source, so it is as if the Prophet (ﷺ) himself took charge of everything that came from it, and the first meaning is the more prominent. What is mentioned in the verse is his own people (qawm), the kind of people among whom he was sent. As for those to whom he was sent, the verse says nothing about them either by negation or affirmation, though he is mentioned as sent to them in other verses. The specificity of the people does not contradict the generality of that, so there is no difficulty in restricting the "others" to being of the unlettered in lineage, that is, Arabs.

It has been said that the intended meaning of the unlettered is unlettered in the sense of illiteracy, so that it includes non-Arabs (ʿajam). Mujahid interpreted it this way, as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from him. This was objected to on the grounds that non-Arabs were not unlettered.

It has also been said that the intended meaning is being attributed to a nation (umma) in general, not being unable to read and write. This is as you see. But this interpretation is not troubled by what al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group of others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We were sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when Surat al-Jumu'ah was revealed, and he recited it. When he reached ﴿wa-akharina minhum lamma yalhaqu bihim﴾, a man said to him: 'O Messenger of God, who are these who have not yet joined us?' He placed his hand on Salman al-Farisi (may God be pleased with him) and said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, if faith were at the Pleiades, men from these would attain it.'" By this, the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated that they are Persians. It is well known that they are not unlettered in the sense of lineage among Arabs.

Some scholars said: the intended meaning of the unlettered is in contrast to the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), since most of them did not concern themselves with reading and writing, because they had no heavenly scripture whose knowledge would call them to that. Thus it includes the Persians, since they had no scripture, just as the Arabs had none. On this basis, the hadith's indication of interpreting the "others" as Persians is explained. It is nevertheless a case of illustration (bab al-tamthil), and the mention of only some categories is based on the view that some nations also have no scripture.

It may be said that the ﴿min﴾ in ﴿minhum﴾ is a noun meaning "some of" (bi-ma'na ba'd), functioning as a subject (mubtada'), as was said concerning God's words ﴿wa-min al-nas man yaqulu﴾ (2:8). The plural pronoun refers to ﴿akharina﴾, and the clause ﴿lamma yalhaqu bihim﴾ is the predicate, so it includes the others: groups of people who will join until the Day of Resurrection, from among the Arabs, the Romans, the non-Arabs and others. This is how al-Dahhak, Ibn Hayyan, and Mujahid in one narration interpreted it. In this case the hadith is an instance of restriction and illustration, like Ibn Umar's statement: "They are the people of Yemen," and Ibn Jubayr's statement: "They are the Romans and non-Arabs." So reflect on this.

Some claimed that the intended meaning of God's words ﴿lamma yalhaqu bihim﴾ is that they have not caught up with them in virtue (fadl), because of the excellence of the Companions over the Successors (tabi'un) and those after them. But in this there is a problem: the negation of ﴿lamma﴾ continues up to the present and is expected to be followed by occurrence, so it would indicate that the Successors' and later generations' attaining the virtue of the Companions is expected to happen, though this is not the case. They have stated explicitly that no Successor, however great his rank in virtue, reaches the rank of a Companion, even one who was not among the senior Companions. Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak was asked about Mu'awiyah and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, which of them was better. He said: "The dust that entered the nostril of Mu'awiyah's horse is better in God's sight than a hundred Umars ibn Abd al-Aziz." Mu'awiyah had prayed behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and recited ﴿ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim﴾ (1:6) and so on, and Mu'awiyah said: "Amin." He used as evidence for the non-attainment of the Companions the authentic saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about them: "If one of you spent gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it," on the view that the address is to the whole Umma. As for his (ﷺ) saying: "My Umma is like the rain; one does not know whether its first part is better or its last," this is an exaggeration of their excellence, like the saying of one speaking about a garment of good lining: "One does not know whether its outside is better or its lining."

﴿Dhalika﴾ refers to what preceded of his (ﷺ) being a messenger to the unlettered and to those after them, a teacher and purifier. The sense of distance in it is for glorification: that is, that great virtue ﴿fadlu Allah﴾, His favour and bounty, may He be exalted in glory, ﴿yu'tihi man yasha'u﴾ "He bestows it on whom He wills" from among His servants, by grace. He, glorified be He, does not will to grant it to anyone after him (ﷺ).

﴿Wallahu dhu al-fadl al-'azim﴾, the One whose blessings of this world and the Hereafter are considered insignificant in comparison.

﴿The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah﴾, i.e., who were taught it and charged with acting upon what is in it. The word "entrusted" (tahmil) in this sense is common and approaches literal usage. The intended people are the Jews. ﴿Then they did not carry it﴾, i.e., they did not act upon what is in its contents, among which are the verses that clearly testify to the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿Like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾, i.e., large books, as the indefinite form suggests. The choice of the word "safar" (books), which contains the meaning of uncovering knowledge, [indicates] one who wearies himself carrying them and does not benefit from them. ﴿And carrying﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to "the donkey," since it is definite in form while the operative element in it is the meaning of "example," or it is an adjective (ṣifa) for it, because its definiteness is mental (dhihni), so it has the meaning of an indefinite noun and is described by what indefinite nouns are described by, according to the more correct view.

Abu Hayyan attributed to the scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) that the circumstantial clause is definite in such a construction. The connection of the verse to what precedes it is that it implies that this Messenger who was sent, Allah has sent him with the characteristics attributed to him in the Torah and on the tongues of the prophets of the Children of Israel, as if it were said: "He is the one who sent the one given good news of in the Torah, described in it as the unlettered Prophet sent to a nation of unlettered people, [like] the one who was given his description in it and knew it, then did not believe in him, like the donkey." In the verse there is evidence of the bad state of the scholar who does not act upon his knowledge. The specification of the carrier by the comparison to it is because it is like knowledge in ignorance. Among this is the saying of the poet:

"Those who hope for journeys, they have no knowledge of their paths, except as the knowledge of camels."

"By your life, the camel does not know, when it goes out in the morning, with its loads, or when it returns in the evening, what is in the panniers."

This is based on what is transmitted from Ibn Khalawayh that "al-ba'ir" (camel) is among the names of the donkey, like "al-jamal al-bazil." Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Zayd ibn Ali read "ḥamalū" (they carried) in the active voice. Abdullah read "ḥimārin" (a donkey) indefinite. It is also read "yuḥammalu" with the shadda on the mim, in the passive voice.

﴿Evil is the example of the people who denied the signs of Allah﴾, i.e., evil is the example of the people, the example of those who denied. The annexed noun (muḍāf) has been omitted, and it is the specified term of dispraise (al-makhsus bil-dhamm), and the annexed-to noun (muḍāf ilayh) has been placed in its position. It is permissible that "alladhina" (those who) be an adjective of "al-qawm" (the people), and the specified term is omitted, meaning: evil is the example of the people who denied the signs of Allah, it. The pronoun refers back to ﴿the example of those who were entrusted with the Torah﴾.

The apparent meaning of the words of al-Kashshaf is that the specified term is the mentioned "example," and the agent is concealed, explained by an omitted specification (tamyiz), and the estimate is: "evil is an example, the example of the people," etc. It was objected that Sibawayh explicitly stated that the specification which explains the concealed pronoun in the chapter of "ni'ma" cannot be omitted, and even if its permissibility were granted, it would be rare. It was answered that this is a clarification of the resultant meaning, and it is closer to considering the first view. Ibn Atiyyah's statement, "the estimate is: evil is the example, the people," is from that chapter; otherwise it would involve omitting the agent, and they have said it is not permissible except in specific cases, and this is not one of them.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., those who place denial in the place of affirmation, or those who wrong themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment because of denial.

Say, "O you who have become Jews" (*hadu*): that is, who have adopted Judaism, meaning who have become Jews. ﴿If you claim that you are friends of God﴾: that is, beloved to Him, glorified is He. He did not attribute *awliya'* (friends) to Himself, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Surely the friends of God...﴾ [Yunus 10:62]. Al-Tayyibi said: this indicates the distinction between one who claims friendship and one whom the Mighty and Majestic specifically designates for it. ﴿Apart from other people﴾: this is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) referring to the pronoun that returns to the subject of *in* (if). That is, ﴿passing over people﴾ [i.e., to the exclusion of others].

﴿Then wish for death﴾: that is, then ask God, exalted is He, to cause you to die and to transfer you from the abode of trial to the place of honour. ﴿If you are truthful﴾: its answer (*jawab*) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. That is, if you are truthful in your claim and certain that it is true, then wish for death, for whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise loves to be delivered from this abode, which is the dwelling-place of sorrows and troubles. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to say this to them, to demonstrate their lie. For they used to say: ﴿We are the sons of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:18], and they claimed that the Hereafter belonged exclusively to them with God, and they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews﴾ [al-Baqara 2:111].

It is related that when the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, became prominent, the Jews of Medina wrote to the Jews of Khaybar: "If you follow Muhammad, we will obey him; and if you oppose him, we will oppose him." They said: "We are the sons of the Friend of the Merciful (Abraham), and among us are 'Uzayr, the son of God, and the prophets. When has prophethood ever been among the Arabs? We have more right to it than Muhammad, and there is no way to follow him." Then the verse ﴿Say, "O you who have become Jews"...﴾ was revealed.

The use of *in*, which denotes doubt, together with *za'amtum* (you claim), is meant to indicate that one should not be definite about it, since there is that which refutes it.

Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿*fatamannu al-mawita*﴾ with a kasra on the *waw*, likening it to the *waw* in ﴿*law istata'na*﴾ (if we were able). It is also reported from Ibn al-Sumayfa' that he read it with a fatha on the *waw*. Al-Kisa'i related that some Bedouins read it with a *hamza*, vowelled with a damma, in place of the *waw*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 62, verse 7:

﴿And they will never wish for it (death), ever.﴾ This is a report of their future state, namely that they will not wish for death. This is specific to those addressed (the Jews), as a group has explicitly stated. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "By He in whose hand is my soul, none of you will say it (wish for death) except that he will choke on his saliva." So none of them wished for it. This was only because they were certain of his truthfulness (peace and blessings be upon him), so they knew that if they wished for it, they would die on the spot and the threat would befall them. This is one of the miracles.

The negation of this wish appears in another verse with "lan" (never). This is a matter of stylistic variation (tafannun), according to the well-known view that both "la" and "lan" negate the future without emphasis. As for the one who holds that "lan" conveys emphasis, the reason for the emphasis being specific to that position is that they claimed exclusivity over the people in both positions, and they added there that it is a manifest matter with no doubt, firmly established before Allah, so it was fitting to emphasize what negates it.

The "bi" in His words, glorified is He: ﴿بِما قَدَّمَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ [bi-ma qaddamat aydihim, "because of what their hands have sent forward"] is causal, related to what the negation indicates, i.e., they refuse to wish for it because of what their hands have sent forward. It was also permitted that it be connected to the negation itself, as if it were said: their wishing was negated because of what their hands sent forward, just as this was said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿ما أنْتَ بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ بِمَجْنُونٍ﴾ [al-Qalam: 2] ("You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman"). What is meant by "what their hands have sent forward" is disbelief and the sins that necessitate entry into the Fire. Since the hand, among the limbs of a human being, is the locus of most of his actions, it is expressed sometimes as the self and sometimes as power. ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِالظَّالِمِينَ﴾ [And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers], i.e., of them. The choice of explicit mention over pronoun is for their censure and for recording upon them that they are wrongdoers in everything they do and omit, among the matters of which is their claim to what they are far removed from. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it, confirming what it indicated of the evil of their deeds and its requiring punishment, i.e., Allah, exalted is He, knows what has issued from them of the various kinds of wrongdoing and sins, and what will come from them, and He will requite them for that.

﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee﴾ and do not dare to wish for, out of fear that you will be seized by the consequences of your deeds, ﴿then indeed it will meet you﴾ without fail, with no averting it and no turning it back. The clause is the predicate of *inna* (the particle of emphasis), and the *fa'* (then) is used because the noun contains the meaning of a conditional through its description by the relative clause. The adjective and the noun it describes are like one thing. So it should not be said that *fa'* enters the predicate only when the subject contains the meaning of a conditional, and that the thing containing this meaning is the relative pronoun, which is not a subject. Its entry into such a construction is not obligatory, as its entry into a true answer (*jawab*) is. It occurs only for a purpose suited to the context, and here the purpose is to stress that escape is impossible. Fleeing from a thing, in the normal course of things, is a cause of failing to escape it, so *fa'* is brought to indicate that fleeing is the cause of meeting it, as an intensification of what was mentioned and a reversal of the situation. It has been said that what follows the *fa'* is an answer in meaning, in the sense of informing, so that the fleeing, which is thought to be a cause of safety, becomes a cause of being informed of meeting it, as in His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [an-Nahl 16:53]. This is a weak view in our case, since there is no intensification in it in terms of meaning. A group, among them al-Farra' (al-Farra'), denied that *fa'* enters such a construction, and said it is here superfluous. It is also permitted that the relative clause be the predicate of *inna*, and the *fa'* be coordinating, as if it were said: "Indeed, death is the thing from which you flee, so it will meet you."

Zayd ibn 'Ali (Zayd ibn 'Ali) read ﴿innahu mulaqikum﴾ without *fa'*, and this is explained as the predicate being the relative clause, and this sentence being a new (independent) sentence, or the predicate being the sentence and the relative clause being a qualifier, as in the reading of the majority. It is also permitted that the predicate be ﴿mulaqikum﴾ and *innahu* be an emphasis for *inna al-mawt* (indeed death), because the speech has been long, so the particle is emphasized with the pronoun referring to the noun that follows *inna*. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿tafirruna minhu mulaqikum﴾ without *fa'* and without *innahu*, and this is clear.

﴿Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ who is not hidden from Him anything hidden. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ of disbelief and disobedience, by recompensing you for it. More than one (scholar) has inferred from the verse the blame of fleeing from the plague (*ta'un*). The discussion of this is lengthy. Some of them have declared it forbidden, such as Ibn Khuzaymah (Ibn Khuzaymah), for he titled a chapter in his *Sahih*: "The chapter on fleeing from the plague being one of the major sins, and that Allah Most High punishes whoever commits it, unless He pardons him." He cited the hadith of 'A'ishah (ﷺ?): "Fleeing from the plague is like fleeing from the battlefield." It was narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Tabarani (al-Tabarani), Ibn 'Adi (Ibn 'Adi) and others, and its chain is good.

Al-Taj al-Subki (al-Taj al-Subki) mentioned that most (scholars) hold it to be forbidden, and some said it is disliked, such as Imam Malik (Malik). Qadi 'Iyad (Qadi 'Iyad) and others related the permissibility of leaving the land in which the plague occurs, from a group of the Companions, among them Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (Abu Musa al-Ash'ari) and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, and from the Successors, among them al-Aswad ibn Hilal and Masruq. Imam Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated that 'Amr ibn al-'As said in his sermon, concerning the plague, at the end of it: "This is a scourge like a flood; whoever avoids it, it misses him, and like fire; whoever avoids it, it misses him; and whoever remains, it burns him." In another wording: "Indeed this plague is a filth, so they scattered from it into the ravines and these valleys, and they scattered." This reached 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he did not disapprove of it nor disliked it. And from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: "We used to converse with Abu Musa al-Ash'ari while he was in his house in Kufa, and when the plague had occurred he said to us: 'There is no blame on you for moving away from this town and going out into the wide expanse of your lands until this calamity is lifted; for I will inform you of what is disliked in that: that one who leaves thinks that if he had stayed and it had struck him, then if he had left he would not have been struck. If he does not think this, then there is no blame on him for leaving and keeping away from it.'"

Al-Bayhaqi (al-Bayhaqi) and others related from him with a good chain that he said: "Indeed this plague has occurred, so whoever wishes to keep away from it, let him do so. And beware of two things: that someone says, 'A person left and was safe, and a person sat and was struck; if I had left, I would have been safe as so-and-so was safe, and if I had sat, I would have been struck as so-and-so was struck.'" It is understood from this that there is no harm in leaving, while believing that every decree will certainly come to pass. And it seems to me that you choose this. However, in the fatawa (legal rulings) of the scholar Ibn Hajar (Ibn Hajar) it is stated that the point of dispute is when one leaves fleeing from it, believing that if he were to remain, it would strike him, and that his fleeing will not save him, but he leaves hoping to be saved. As for leaving his place with the intention that he has the power to escape the decree of Allah Most High, and that his action is what saves him, it is clear that this is forbidden, indeed it is disbelief by consensus.

As for leaving due to an impediment of business, or for treatment of an illness contracted, or other than that, this is something concerning which there should be no dispute as to its permissibility, as some verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) have stated. Among this, in my view, is the occurrence of a natural anxiety in him that he cannot repel, which harms him clearly, and a strong supposition that he will not be buried or washed if he dies in that place. It has been said: the fleeing from other than the plague, of other destructive things, is not analogized to fleeing from the plague, for it is commanded. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti (al-Jalal al-Suyuti) said: "Fleeing from epidemic disease, like fever, and from all other causes of death, is permissible by consensus, and the plague is excepted from the general category of destructive things from which fleeing is commanded, because of the prohibition, whether prohibitive or reprehensible, of fleeing from it. They differed concerning the cause of the prohibition. It has been said: it is that if the plague occurs in a city, for example, it spreads to all who are in it through the entry of its cause, so fleeing from it is of no benefit; rather, if his term has come, he dies, whether he leaves or not; and if not, then not. And if he remains, then remaining is required, because leaving involves futility which is not fitting for the sensible." This was objected to by denying its generality, for when it occurs in a city, all who are in it are affected by the entry of its cause; and even if it is granted, the epidemic is like it in that a person who is in his city, if his term has come, he dies, and if he leaves, then he lives, and if not, then not, and if he remains... yet they permitted fleeing from it.

It has also been said: the cause is that if people all rushed to leave, the sick who are unable to leave would be lost for lack of one who attends to them, and the dead for lack of one who prepares them; and also, in the departure of the strong there is a breaking of the hearts of the weak who are unable to leave; and also, the one leaving says, "If I do not leave, I will die," and the one remaining says, "If I left, I would be safe," so both fall into the *law* (regret, "if only") which is forbidden. This was objected to, since all of that is also present in fleeing from an epidemic in general. Likewise the disease that is newly appearing, known among people as *Abu Zau'ah*, whose treatment baffled physicians, and in which precautionary measures and isolation in the known manner used for the plague were of no benefit. It has also been said: the cause is that for one who dies of it, and likewise for the patient, seeking reward, who remains in his place, even if he does not die from it, there is the reward of a martyr; and in fleeing there is turning away from martyrdom, and this is the point of comparison in the hadith of 'A'ishah according to some. This was objected to by saying that it is established that "he (ﷺ) passed by a leaning wall and hastened, and no one was prevented from that." Likewise (the case of) fleeing from fire, although the one who dies by it is also a martyr. Some scholars held that the prohibition is devotional (*ta'abbudi*), and it seems that he, seeing that no cause for it is free from criticism, said that. They have numerous treatises on this question; whoever wishes to complete the discussion on it should return to them.

"O you who have believed, when the call is proclaimed for prayer" (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إذا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلاةِ﴾): that is, the call is made for it, i.e. the adhan (the call to prayer). According to what al-Zamakhshari reports in al-Kashshaf, the intended adhan is the one given when the imam sits on the minbar (pulpit). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had one muezzin (adhan-caller). When he sat on the minbar, the muezzin would call the adhan at the door of the mosque, and when he (ﷺ) descended, he would give the iqama (the call to begin the prayer). Then Abu Bakr and Umar continued in this practice until the time of Uthman, when the people became numerous and the dwellings spread apart. He added another muezzin and ordered the first adhan to be called from his house, which was called al-Zawra'. When he sat on the minbar, the second muezzin would call the adhan, and when he descended, he would give the iqama. This was not criticised.

In the hadith transmitted by the group (all except Muslim): "When it was the time of Uthman and the people increased, he added a third call (nida') at al-Zawra'." In a narration of al-Bukhari and Muslim: "He added the second call." Both have the same meaning. The naming of what is done as first or second adhan is by reference to the fact that it did not exist in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) but came later. It is called "third" because the iqama is also called adhan, as in the hadith: "Between every two adhans there is a prayer." 

The Hanafi mufti of the exalted Ottoman domain, the virtuous Sa'd Allah Jalabi, said: What is considered in the application of the command, namely the verse of His that follows, "﴿فاسْعَوْا﴾ (then hasten)," is the first adhan, according to the more correct view in our school, because the notification is achieved by it, not by the adhan before the minbar. This was refuted: the first (adhan) did not exist in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), as you have heard, so how can it be said that the intended one is "the first according to the more correct view"? As for the second not involving notification, this does no harm, because its time is known approximately. If what was mentioned were intended, then the hastening would be obligatory by the first and trade would be forbidden, but this is not the case.

In Kitab al-Ahkam it is narrated from Ibn Umar and al-Hasan regarding His saying "﴿إذا نُودِيَ﴾ (when it is called)" etc., that he said: "When the imam comes out and the muezzin calls the adhan, then it has been called for prayer." End of quote. This is the transmitted tafsir, so nothing else is to be taken into account, thus said al-Khafaji.

In the books of the Hanafis there is a contrary view. In al-Kanz (Kanz al-Daqa'iq) and its commentary: "Hastening and abandoning trade become obligatory at the first adhan, due to His saying: '﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إذا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلاةِ﴾ (O you who have believed, when the call is proclaimed for prayer)' etc.; it is taken into account only because notification is achieved by it. This view is the correct one in the school. It has been said: the consideration is for the second adhan, which is before the minbar, because in his time there was only that one. This is weak, because if it were taken into account for the obligation of hastening, one would not be able to perform the pre-prayer sunna or attend the sermon, and it could even be feared that one would miss the Friday prayer." End of quote. Many similar statements exist, but the objection to it is strong, so reflect.

"From the day of Friday" (﴿مِن يَوْمِ الجُمُعَةِ﴾): that is, in it, as in His saying: "﴿أرُونِي ماذا خَلَقُوا مِنَ الأرْضِ﴾ (Show me what they have created of the earth)" [Fatir 40], that is, in it. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that "min" be partitive (lil-tab'id). In al-Kashshaf it is explanatory (bayan) of "idha" and an elucidation of it. The apparent meaning is that he intended the well-known explanatory use, so an objection was raised: the condition for explanatory "min" is that what follows can be taken as the thing explained before it, and this is absent here, because the whole cannot be taken as the part, and "the day" cannot here mean general time, because "Friday" is a proper name for the known day and is not used for anything else in custom, and there is no indication of that here. It has been said that he intended the linguistic explanation, namely to explain that this time falls on some day of the days, since "idha" contains ambiguity; so it is compatible with the meaning "in", and with partitive use. But this, as you see, is far-fetched.

"Al-Jumu'a" (Friday) with a damma on the mim is the most eloquent, most common and widespread, and with it the majority read. Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-A'mash read it with sukun (al-Jum'a). It is narrated from Abu 'Amr, and it is the dialect of Tamim, and the fatha has come but is not recited with it. Some have also transmitted the kasra. They mentioned that "al-Juma'a" with damma is like "al-Juma'a" with sukun. Its meaning is "the gathered" (al-majmu'), i.e. the day of the gathered group, like their saying "dihka" for "one laughed at". As for "al-Juma'a" with fatha, its meaning is "the gathering" (al-jami'), i.e. the day of the gathering time, like their saying "dihka" for "one who laughs much". Abu al-Baqa' said: "al-Juma'a" with two dammas, and with sukun on the mim, is a verbal noun meaning "gathering". 

It has been said: in the dwelling (al-maskan), it means "that in which people gather", like "rajul duhka" (a man who is laughed at much). End of quote. The day of Friday has become a proper name for the known day of the week. The apparent wording of most lexicographers is that "al-Juma'a" alone, without "day", became a proper name for it, and there is no obstacle to this. The idafa (construction) of the general to the specific ("al-yawm" to "al-Juma'a") is permissible and commendable when the second is obscure, as here, because the naming is recent, as you will know, God willing. So it is not ugly, like the idafa in "insan Zayd" (a human, Zayd).

The Arabs, as many have said, used to call Friday "'Aruba." It is said that it is a proper name of the genus (alam jins), used with the article and without it. It has been said that the article is obligatory. Al-Khafaji said: The first is more correct.

In al-Nihaya of Ibn al-Athir: "'Aruba is an old name for Friday, and it seems it is not Arabic. It is said: 'the day of 'Aruba' and 'the day of al-'Aruba'. The more eloquent is that the article does not enter it." End of quote. What he thought, that it is not Arabic, was asserted by the Mukhtasar of Kitab al-Tadhyil wal-Takmil, on words borrowed into use, by Jamal al-Din 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad known as al-Shishi, who said: "'Aruba, indefinite and definite, is the day of Friday; it is a Syriac, Arabicised noun." Then he said: al-Suhayli said: "The meaning of 'Aruba is mercy, according to what has reached us from some people of knowledge." End of quote. This is strange, so let it be remembered.

The first to name it "Jum'a" is said to have been Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy. 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Sirin, who said: "The people of Madina gathered before the Prophet (ﷺ) came and before the Friday prayer was revealed. The Ansar said: 'The Jews have a day in every seven days in which they gather, and the Christians likewise. Come, let us make for ourselves a day in which we gather, so we remember Allah and thank Him.' They said: 'Saturday is for the Jews, and Sunday for the Christians. So make it the day of 'Aruba.' They used to call Friday by that name. They gathered to As'ad ibn Zurara, and he led them in two rak'as that day and reminded them. So they named it 'Jum'a' when they gathered to him. He slaughtered a sheep for them, and they ate their lunch and dinner from it, and that was for the common people. Then Allah revealed about that afterwards: '﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إذا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلاةِ﴾ (O you who have believed, when the call is proclaimed for prayer)' etc."

That As'ad was the first to gather (the people) is also transmitted from other than Ibn Sirin. Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b that his father, whenever he heard the call on Friday, would invoke mercy on As'ad ibn Zurara. I said: "O father, what is this seeking of forgiveness for As'ad ibn Zurara every time you hear the adhan for Friday?" He said: "Because he was the first who gathered us in Naqi' al-Khadamat, from the lava-field of Bani Bayada." I said: "How many were you that day?" He said: "Forty men."

The apparent meaning of Ibn Sirin's words, "Then Allah revealed about that afterwards: '﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾' etc.," is that As'ad established the Friday prayer before it was made obligatory. Likewise his saying: "The people of Madina gathered before the Prophet (ﷺ) came and before the Friday prayer was revealed." In Fath al-Qadir this is stated explicitly. The allamah Ibn Hajar in Tuhfat al-Muhtaj said: "It was made obligatory, i.e. the Friday prayer, in Makka, but we did not establish it there because of lack of the required number, or because its sign is public display, and the Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform it secretly there. The first to establish it in Madina before the Hijra was As'ad ibn Zurara, in a village at a mile from Madina." End of quote. Perhaps it was made obligatory, and then its verse was revealed, like the wudu' for prayer, for it was first made obligatory in Makka along with prayer, then its verse was revealed. But this is disturbed by what Ibn Majah transmitted from Jabir, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a khutba (sermon) and said: "Allah has made the Friday prayer obligatory upon you in this place of mine, on this day of mine, in this month of mine, in this year of mine, until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever abandons it out of contempt for it or denial of it, Allah will not gather his affairs, nor bless his matter. Beware: there is no prayer for him, no zakat for him, no hajj for him, no fasting for him, and no righteousness for him until he repents. Whoever repents, Allah will accept his repentance." For the apparent meaning is that this khutba was in Madina. Indeed the apparent meaning of the report is that it was long after the Hijra, since the apparent meaning of his (ﷺ) saying in it, "there is no hajj for him," is that hajj was obligatory at that time. Although it is disputed when hajj became obligatory: it is said it was made obligatory before the Hijra, it is said in its first year, it is said in its second, and so on up to the tenth. But they said that the most correct is that it was made obligatory in the sixth year. So either this casts doubt on the authenticity of the hadith, or it is said that its import is the obligation of the Friday prayer until the Day of Resurrection, i.e. with this condition. And it is said that what existed before its obligation was not restricted by this condition.

Then what was mentioned, that As'ad was the first to gather in Madina, is contradicted by what al-Tabarani transmitted from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: "The first of the emigrants to arrive in Madina was Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, and he was the first to gather people there on Friday. He gathered them before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived, and they were twelve men."

Al-Bukhari, as al-Suyuti transmitted, similarly (reported), and this was by his (ﷺ) command. For al-Daraqutni transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) gave permission for the Friday prayer before he migrated, and he could not gather (people) in Makka. So he wrote to Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr: 'To proceed: look for the day on which the Jews chant the Zabur aloud. Gather your women and children. When the sun declines from its midpoint at the zawal (midday) on Friday, draw near to Allah with two rak'as.'" He said: "So he was the first to gather, until the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madina, and he gathered at the zawal of the Zuhr and made it public."

So perhaps what indicates that As'ad was the first to gather is more established than these reports; or it may be reconciled by saying that As'ad was the first to establish it without a command from him (ﷺ), as the report of Ibn Sirin indicates, and Ibn al-Humam stated this explicitly; and Mus'ab was the first to establish it by his command (ﷺ). Or it may be said that Mus'ab was the first to establish it in Madina itself, and As'ad was the first to establish it in a village near Madina. The saying "in Madina" is loose. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: The two reports may be reconciled by saying that As'ad was the amir and Mus'ab was the imam. This is as you see. But none of the reports I have examined states explicitly who established it before the Hijra in Madina with the khutba, which is one of its conditions. Ibn Sirin's report hints at it with his words "and reminded them." It may also be said that the Friday prayer is a technical (shar'i) term for the prayer that fulfils its conditions, so whenever it is said that so-and-so was the first to pray the Friday prayer, this implies the fulfilment of the conditions. But it is very far-fetched that what As'ad, may Allah be pleased with him, did, if it was before its obligation, fulfilled what is now known of its conditions. Then I do not know whether As'ad prayed the Zuhr that day or was content with the two rak'as he prayed in its place. And if he was content, how was that permitted for him without his (ﷺ) command? The most that can be supposed is that the Ansar knew of the obligation of the Friday prayer in Makka and knew its conditions and that it replaces the Zuhr prayer, so they wished to perform it before they were commanded specifically, so their elite made their common people desire it in the best manner, and they came to As'ad, and he led them in prayer. This is very contrary to the apparent meaning, so reflect. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 62, verse 9 (part 2 of 2):

As for what was from his (ﷺ) prayer of Jumu'ah (the Friday prayer) on it, it has been narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah as an emigrant, he alighted at Quba with the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf and stayed there on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and he founded their mosque. Then he set out on Friday for Madinah, and the time of the Jumu'ah prayer overtook him among the Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, in the bottom of a valley belonging to them. He delivered the khutbah and led the Jumu'ah prayer, and this was the first Jumu'ah that he (ﷺ) prayed.

Some have said: this day was only named the day of Jumu'ah because Adam (peace be upon him) gathered with Eve on earth on it. It has also been said: because the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) was gathered on it. This is similar to what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I said, "O Prophet of Allah, why was the day of Jumu'ah named so?" He said: "Because on it the clay of your father Adam (peace be upon him) was gathered," and the report continues. This indicates that the naming was before Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy. The angels call it, on the Day of Resurrection, the Day of Increase (yawm al-mazid), because Allah, exalted is He, manifests Himself on it to the people of Paradise, and gives them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human, as in a hadith narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). And it is among the best of days.

In a report narrated by many, including Imam Ahmad and Ibn Majah, from Abu Lubabah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The day of Jumu'ah is the lord of days and greater in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, than the day of al-Fitr and the day of al-Adha." In it are also: that Adam was created on it, his descent to the earth, his death, and the hour of response (sa'at al-ijabah), i.e., for supplication, so long as it is not a supplication for something haram, and the Hour (qiyam al-sa'ah) will occur on it. In the report of al-Tabarani: "On it he entered Paradise and on it he came out of it."

Ibn Hibban authenticated the report: "The sun does not rise or set on a day better than the day of Jumu'ah." In the report of Muslim: "On it Adam was created, on it he was admitted to Paradise, on it he was removed from it, on it the Hour will occur, and it is the best day on which the sun has risen." And the report is authentic: "On it he was forgiven, and on it he died."

Ahmad took from the two reports of Muslim and Ibn Hibban that it is better even than the day of 'Arafah. Many of the Hanbalis preferred its night over the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr). It has been said: these two have specific proofs, so they take precedence.

There has been disagreement about specifying the hour of response on it. From Abu Burdah: it is when the imam stands in the prayer until he finishes from it. From al-Hasan: it is at the decline of the sun (zawal). From al-Sha'bi: it is between the prohibition of trade and its permissibility. From 'A'ishah: it is when the caller calls to prayer. In a marfu' hadith transmitted by Ibn Abi Shaybah from Kathir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani: it is from the iqamah of the prayer until the dismissal from it. From Abu Umamah: "I truly hope that the hour in Jumu'ah is one of these hours: when the muezzin calls the adhan, or when the imam sits on the minbar, or at the iqamah." From Tawus and Mujahid: it is after the 'Asr. It has been said other than this, but the specification of the majority has not been authenticated. Allah, exalted is He, has concealed it, just as He concealed the Greatest Name, the Night of Power and other things, for a wisdom that is not hidden.

Page 102

﴿So hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾: that is, walk toward it without excessive haste. In the hadith the contrast of sa'y (striving) with mashy (walking) has come, and this was placed among the particulars of Jumu'ah. The Six (compilers of the canonical books) transmitted in their books from Abu Salamah, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, said: "When the prayer is established, do not come to it while you are hastening; come to it while you are walking, and upon you is tranquility (al-sakinah). What you catch, pray, and what you miss, complete."

The remembrance of Allah is taken to mean the khutbah and the prayer. It has been favoured that what is meant is the prayer, and it is allowed that what is meant is the khutbah, which, according to what has been said, is majaz (figurative usage) from mentioning a part for the whole, as with its application to the prayer, or because the khutbah is like the place for it. It has been said: the remembrance is general, including the well-known khutbah and something like a tasbihah. The Hanafis used the verse as evidence, according to Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, that for the khutbah of Jumu'ah, which is a condition for its validity, mere remembrance suffices, and a lengthy one is not required; its minimum is the amount of the tashahhud, as his two companions required. They explained this: He, exalted is He, mentioned "remembrance" without distinguishing between a lengthy remembrance called a khutbah and a remembrance not called a khutbah. So the condition is the more general remembrance, determined by what is definitive. However, what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) is his choosing one of the two forms, namely the remembrance called khutbah, and his constancy in it, so that was obligatory or a sunnah, not that it is the condition beyond which nothing else suffices, since it would not then be an explanation of the non-ambiguity of the word "remembrance." The Shafi'is require two khutbahs, which have pillars (arkan) in their view, and they used reports as evidence for this. In any case, the command to strive is for obligation.

It has been used as evidence for the obligation of Jumu'ah, since the command to strive to the remembrance of Allah is arranged upon the call to prayer. If the prayer is meant, or both prayer and khutbah, then it is evident; likewise if the khutbah is meant, because the obligation of striving to a condition, which is itself intended for something else, follows the obligation of that something else. Do you not see that one on whom the prayer is not obligatory is not obligated to strive to Jumu'ah, by consensus? Likewise its obligation is established by the Sunnah and consensus. Some Hanafis stated that it is the most emphatic obligation, more than Zuhr, and that its denier is an unbeliever, and it is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). It has been said it is a collective obligation (fard kifayah), but this is an anomalous view. In a hadith narrated by Abu Dawud, and Al-Nawawi said it is on the condition of al-Shaykhayn: "Jumu'ah is a binding right upon every Muslim in congregation, except four: a slave, a woman, a child, or a sick person."

They agreed on the requirement of a number for it, because of this report and others. The words of al-Qashani, that it is valid with one who is not counted, as in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, but they differed about the amount, in several views:

First: it is two, one of whom is the imam, the view of al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih and Dawud.
Second: three, one of whom is the imam, reported from al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and from Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and al-Rafi'i and others related it from the older view of al-Shafi'i.
Third: four, one of whom is the imam, held by Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri and al-Layth, related by Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Awza'i and Abu Thawr, which he preferred, related in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab from Muhammad, and the author of al-Talkhis related it as an older opinion of al-Shafi'i.
Fourth: seven, related from 'Ikrimah.
Fifth: nine, related from Rabi'ah.
Sixth: twelve, and in one report from Rabi'ah; al-Mawardi related it from Muhammad, al-Zuhri and al-Awza'i.
Seventh: thirteen, one of whom is the imam, related from Ishaq ibn Rahawayh.
Eighth: twenty, narrated by Ibn Habib from Malik.
Ninth: thirty, in one report from Malik.
Tenth: forty, one of whom is the imam, held by 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah and Imam al-Shafi'i in his new view, which is the well-known position of Imam Ahmad, and one of the two reported views from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz.
Eleventh: fifty, in the other report from him.
Twelfth: eighty, related by al-Mazari.
Thirteenth: a large group without a specified limit, which is the school of Malik. It is well known that he said: no specific number is required, but rather a congregation sufficient to make a village inhabited, among whom trade takes place; it is not valid with three, four or the like.
