Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in his commentary on al-Bukhari: "Perhaps this school is the strongest of the schools in terms of evidence." I say: the strongest of them is the school of Imam Abu Hanifah. Al-Muzani, one of the great transmitters from al-Shafi'i, preferred it, and it is the choice of Jalal al-Suyuti. The reason for his choice, together with mention of the evidence for most views, for and against, is recorded in a treatise he named "The Light of the Candle concerning the Number for Jumu'ah," and were it not for excessive length I would have mentioned its summary. Whoever wishes that should refer to it, so that the reality of the matter becomes clear to him by its light.

Many of the Companions and Successors read "fa-imdu" (then proceed), and it was taken as an interpretation, on the basis that striving does not mean hastening in walking; it was not treated as Qur'an, because it contradicts the consensus written text of the Mushaf. ﴿And leave off trade﴾: that is, abandon dealing, on the basis that "trade" is figurative for that, so it covers buying, selling, renting and other dealings; or it indicates what is other than it by the indication of the text, and this is perhaps the better view. The command is for obligation, so all of that is forbidden. Indeed it has been reported from 'Ata' the prohibition of permissible play, of a man going to his wife, and of writing a document as well.

Some expressed it as disliked (makruh), and it was taken to mean makruh tahrimi (prohibited-disliked). The statement of al-Akmal in Sharh al-Manar that the disliking is tanzihi (reprehensible but not prohibited) is rejected; and it seems derived from the claim of al-Qadi al-Isbijabi that the command in the verse is for recommendation, which is a false claim according to most of the imams. The general body of scholars holds the sale to be valid, even though it is forbidden, similar to what they said about prayer in a stolen garment or on stolen land. Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is invalid. Mujahid expressed it as "rejected" (mardud). The period of prohibition continues until the imam finishes the prayer. Its beginning is either the time of the khutbah's adhan, reported from al-Zuhri and held by a group, or the beginning of the time of zawal, reported from 'Ata', al-Dahhak and al-Hasan. The apparent view is that those commanded to leave trade are those commanded to strive to the prayer.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim that al-Qasim entered upon his family on Friday, and with them there was a perfume seller whom they were dealing with; they bought from him, and al-Qasim went out to Jumu'ah, found the imam had already gone out, and when he returned he ordered them to cancel the sale. Its apparent meaning is the prohibition of trade when the call to prayer is made, even on one not obligated to it, and the apparent view is the prohibition of buying and selling during the striving.

In al-Siraj al-Wahhaj it is stated that it is not forbidden if it does not occupy one. ﴿That﴾: that is, what was mentioned of striving to the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and leaving off trade, ﴿is better for you﴾: more beneficial than engaging in trade, for the benefit of the Hereafter is more majestic and more lasting. It has been said: it is more beneficial than that and than abandoning striving. The establishment of the basic benefit for the one preferred over is in view of it being a worldly benefit, and it does not indicate that the command is for recommendation and desirability rather than binding obligation, as is not hidden. ﴿If you should know﴾: the good and the bad in their true sense; or, if you are among the people of knowledge, with the verb placed in the position of an intransitive one.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 62, verse 10:**

﴿Then when the prayer has been concluded﴾, i.e., performed and finished, ﴿disperse throughout the land﴾ to attend to your affairs, ﴿and seek of Allah's bounty﴾, i.e., profit, according to what has been said. Makhul, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Musayyab said: what is commanded to be sought is knowledge.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "They were not commanded to anything of seeking the world. It is only visiting a sick person, attending a funeral, and visiting a brother for the sake of Allah, the Exalted." Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). The command here is one of permissibility (ibahah) according to the most correct view. Thus, after the prayer is concluded, it is permissible to sit in the mosque, and leaving is not obligatory. This was also narrated from al-Dahhak and Mujahid.

Al-Karmani, in his commentary on al-Bukhari (Sharh al-Bukhari), reported a consensus (al-ittifaq) on this, but there is room for scrutiny in this, for al-Sarakhsi reported the view that it indicates obligation (lil-wujub),
Page 104

and it has been said that it indicates recommendation (lil-nadb). Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, "from Abdullah ibn Busr al-Harrani, who said: 'I saw Abdullah ibn Busr al-Mazini, companion of the Prophet (ﷺ), that when he had prayed Friday prayer, he would go out and wander in the marketplace for a while, then return to the mosque and pray whatever Allah willed him to pray. He was asked: "Why do you do this?" He said: "I saw the master of the messengers (ﷺ) doing this," and he recited this verse: ﴿Then when the prayer has been concluded﴾,'" and so on.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "When you finish on Friday, go out to the door of the mosque and bargain over something, even if you do not buy it." The view of recommendation (nadbiyyah) was also reported from him, and it is the closest and most suitable to the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And remember Allah much﴾, i.e., much remembrance, and do not restrict His remembrance to the prayer, ﴿that you may succeed﴾, so that you may win the good of both abodes.

From what we have mentioned, the weakness of the argument made here, that a command following a prohibition indicates permissibility, becomes known. The verse has also been cited as evidence for placing the sermon (khutbah) before the prayer, and likewise for the absence of a recommendation to pray the sunnah after it in the mosque. The verse contains no indication negating a post-Friday sunnah. The apparent sense of the words of some eminent scholars is that some people denied that Friday has any sunnah at all. It is possible, though remote, that such a person sensed the negation of the post-Friday sunnah from the command to disperse and seek bounty. As for the negation of a pre-Friday sunnah, it was based on what is reported in the Sahih, and it has been mentioned earlier that the call (nida') in his time was made when he sat on the pulpit (minbar). It is known that when the adhan was completed, he (ﷺ) began the sermon, and when he finished it, he began the prayer, so when did they pray the sunnah? This was answered by saying that his going out (ﷺ) was after the zawal (the sun's decline) by necessity, so it is possible that it was after he used to pray the four (rak'ahs). The ruling must be established by this permissible possibility, because of the generality of what is authentically reported: that he (ﷺ) used to pray four rak'ahs when the sun declined. Likewise, it must be applied to them, because they too know the zawal, like the muezzin, and perhaps they even informed him of the time's entry so that he would call the adhan. Whoever said that it is obligatory to come to the Friday prayer only from a place where the call can be heard cited the words of Allah, ﴿When it is called﴾, etc., as evidence. The matter is one of disagreement. Ibn Umar, Abu Hurayrah, Yunus and al-Zuhri said: it is obligatory to come to it from six miles away. It was also said: from five. Rabi'ah said: from four. This was narrated from al-Zuhri and Ibn al-Munkadir.

Malik and al-Layth said: from three. In Bahr Abi Hayyan: Abu Hanifa and his companions said: coming is obligatory upon those within the city (misr) who hear the call or do not hear it, but not upon one who is outside the city, even if he hears the call. From Ibn Umar, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri, Ahmad and Ishaq: it is obligatory upon one who hears the call. From Rabi'ah: upon one who, when he hears it and leaves his house walking, reaches the prayer in time. Likewise, whoever held that it is obligatory to come to it cited this as evidence, whether the permission is general or not, and whether it is established by a ruler, his deputy, or others or not, because He, the Exalted, only linked the obligation of striving (al-sa'y) to the call absolutely. This is what has been said. The detailed investigation of all of this is found in the lengthier books of jurisprudence (furu').

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 62, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed toward it.﴾ Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and a group [of scholars] narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "While the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering the khutbah on Friday, standing, a caravan arrived in Madinah. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hastened toward it until only twelve men remained, among whom were myself, Abu Bakr and Umar. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And when they saw a trade﴾ to the end of the surah."

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn Abbas, [it is reported] that twelve men and seven women remained in the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If they had all gone out, the mosque would have blazed with fire upon them." In a narration from Qatadah [it is reported that he (ﷺ) said]: "By Him in Whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if the last of you had followed the first of you, the valley would have burst into flames upon you." It was also said that only eleven men remained, and they were, as Abu Bakr said, Ghalib ibn Atiyyah: the ten promised [Paradise], and Ammar in one narration and Ibn Mas'ud in another. According to the previous narration, they counted the ten among them too. They counted Bilal and Jabir on account of his earlier statement. Some did not mention Jabir but mentioned Bilal and Ibn Mas'ud, and some mentioned Ammar instead of Ibn Mas'ud. It was also said that only eight remained, and it was said that forty remained. The caravan belonged to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, carrying food, and the people of Madinah had been afflicted by hunger and high prices.

Abu Dawud in his Marasil narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray the Friday [prayer] before the khutbah, like the two Eids, until one Friday when the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering the khutbah, having already prayed the Friday [prayer]. A man entered and said: 'Indeed Dihyah ibn Khalifah has arrived with merchandise, and whenever he arrived his family would greet him with tambourines.' So the people went out, thinking there was nothing wrong in leaving the attendance of the khutbah, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And when they saw﴾ etc." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) placed the khutbah before the prayer on Friday and delayed the prayer. I do not think this report is sound. The apparent position is that the Prophet (ﷺ) always placed its khutbah before the prayer. They have mentioned that the khutbah is a condition for its validity, and a condition precedes the thing it conditions. I have not seen any of the jurists mention that the matter was as this report contains, nor have I found any hadith meeting the conditions of acceptance that includes that. Yes, the scholar Ibn Hajar al-Haytami mentioned that some deviated from the consensus that the khutbah comes before it. And Allah knows best.

Since the verse concerns those who dispersed, and was revealed after that had occurred from them, they said: the "idha" in it has departed from the sense of the future and is used for the past, as in the verse:

And a boon companion whose cup he increases in sweetness, I gave him to drink when the stars had set.

The pronoun is singular because the connective is "aw" (or). The pronoun referring to trade was chosen over amusement because it is the more important and intended, for by amusement is meant what they confronted the caravan with, such as the tambourine and the like. Or because dispersing for trade, when there is need for it and benefit from it, is blameworthy; so what do you think of dispersing toward amusement, which is blameworthy in itself? It was also said: the pronoun refers to the seeing understood from ﴿رَأوْا﴾, which is contrary to the apparent and immediate sense. It was also said: there is an elision in the speech; the original is "when they saw trade, they dispersed toward it, or amusement, they dispersed toward it," and the second is omitted because the first indicates it. This was objected to: after "aw" the pronoun is not needed for each of the two; rather it suffices to return to one of them, so the elision is without need. Al-Tibi said: it is possible to say that the "aw" in ﴿أوْ لَهْوًا﴾ is like it in the verse:

It appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of forenoon, or your form is more beautiful in the eye.

Al-Jawhari said: he means "bal" (rather), so you are [more beautiful]. The pronoun in ﴿إلَيْها﴾ refers to amusement according to meaning. The secret of this is that trade, when it occupies the responsible person from the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, is counted as amusement, and it is counted as bounty if it does not occupy him, as in the verse of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek from the bounty of Allah﴾. End. It is nothing, as is not hidden.

Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ with the pronoun of amusement, and it was read ﴿إلَيْهِما﴾ with the dual pronoun, as in the verse of Allah the Exalted: ﴿If he is rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [An-Nisa 135]. And that is interpreted, because after "aw," since it is for one of two things, the pronoun is not made dual, and likewise the predicate, the circumstance and the description. So according to this reading it has the meaning of "wa" (and), as was said regarding the verse we mentioned. ﴿And they left you standing﴾, i.e., on the pulpit.

It has been used as evidence for the legitimacy of standing during the khutbah, which for the Hanafis is one of its sunnahs, and for the Shafi'is it is a condition in both khutbahs if one is able to do it. Ibn Majah and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked: "Did the Prophet (ﷺ) deliver the khutbah standing or sitting?" He said: "Do you not recite ﴿And they left you standing﴾?" Likewise Ibn Sirin and Abu Ubaydah were asked and both answered with that. The first to deliver the khutbah sitting was Mu'awiyah.

Perhaps that was due to his inability to stand; otherwise he opposed what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to do. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Ibn Umar that "the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to deliver two khutbahs, sitting between them." Abu Hayyan mentioned that the first to rest during the khutbah was Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. It seems he meant by "resting" other than sitting between the two khutbahs, since that was not what the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, did.

﴿Say: What is with Allah is better than amusement and than trade﴾ — for that is a certain, enduring benefit, unlike what is in them of benefit; for the benefit of amusement is not certain but imagined, and the benefit of trade is not enduring. The placing of amusement first is not from placing privation before possession, as it was imagined, but because it is more blameworthy, so it fits to place it first in the context of blame. Ibn Atiyyah said: trade was placed before amusement in the seeing because it is more important, and it was placed later with the comparison so that the soul would first fall upon the clearer [item]; and this is close to what we mentioned.

Al-Tibi said: what was postponed was placed first, and the preposition was repeated to intend generality in each one, and its independence in what is intended from it, to differ from the preceding in unity of meaning, because that was in a specific incident. Shaykh Abd al-Ghani al-Nabulsi, may Allah pardon him, used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of entertainments, because of the elative form which requires establishing the basic goodness of amusement as of trade. You know that this is founded on assumption and imagination. More wondrous than that is his use of the joining of permissible trade with amusement at the beginning of the verse as evidence for that; and the most wondrous of all is that he composed treatises on the permissibility of that which the sect attributed to our master Jalal al-Din al-Rumi employs, revolving around proofs weaker than a gazelle's waist turning on the axis of coquetry in their presence. Among them are lies without any basis which no sensible person would accept or approve. I do not think what they do is anything but a snare for catching the bird of provision, while the ignorant think it a release from the bond of servitude. So beware of inclining toward that, and rely upon Allah the Exalted, the Owner, ﴿And Allah is the best of providers﴾; to Him, glorified is He, strive, and from Him, Mighty and Majestic, seek provision.

It has been used, from what occurred in the incident, as evidence for the least number that counts for a Friday congregation, that it is twelve, based on what is in most of the narrations, that the remaining ones after the dispersal were like that. The point of the evidence is that the number that counts at the start is counted in continuation; so since the Friday prayer was not invalidated by the dispersal of more than twelve, this shows that this number suffices. But in this there is an objection: although that indicates its validity with twelve men without doubt, there is no indication in it that twelve is a condition, nor that it is not valid with fewer than this number. For this is an individual incident, at most in it that they dispersed, twelve men remained, and the Friday prayer was completed with them; and there is nothing in it that if fewer than this number remained, it would not be completed with them.

Regarding what the imam should do if people disperse from him during the Friday prayer, there is disagreement. According to Abu Hanifah, if he remains alone, or with fewer than three men, he begins the Zuhr prayer anew if they leave him before bowing. According to his two companions, if he has pronounced the takbir while they are with him, he continues it. According to Zufar, if they leave before the sitting, it is invalidated, because the number is a condition of beginning, so it must continue, like the time. The two [companions] argue that it is a condition of establishment, so its continuation is not required, like the khutbah. Abu Hanifah's argument is that establishment occurs by beginning the prayer, and that is not completed except by completing the rak'ah, because what is less than it is not prayer; so it must continue until then, unlike the khutbah, because it contradicts the prayer, so its continuation is not required.

The majority of the Shafi'is said: if forty, or some of them, disperse during the prayer, and he does not enter into ihram immediately after their dispersal in the first rak'ah, a number like them who heard the khutbah, the Friday prayer becomes invalid, so they complete it as Zuhr, similar to what Zufar said. In one opinion: it does no harm if two remain with the imam, since the name of congregation exists, for in continuation what is not overlooked at the beginning is overlooked. The full details are in their proper place.

The Shi'ah used this verse to accuse the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that they preferred their worldly life over their hereafter, in that they dispersed toward amusement and trade and turned away from the prayer, which is the pillar of the religion and better than many acts of worship, especially with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is related that this happened many times among them. In reply: the great Companions such as Abu Bakr, Umar and the rest of the ten promised [Paradise] did not disperse; the incident occurred in the early days of the Hijrah, when most of the people had not yet fully adorned themselves with the manners of the Shari'ah; and the people of Madinah had been struck by hunger and high prices, so those who dispersed feared the severity of the matter upon them if others bought what they could live on, had they not dispersed. For this reason Allah the Exalted did not threaten them with the Fire or the like for it, but the most He did was to rebuke, admonish and advise them. As for the report that this occurred from them many times, if it is meant as the narration of al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: "It reached me, and Allah knows best, that they did this three times," then such a thing is not to be given attention, nor is it of high standing among the scholars of hadith. And if something else is meant, let it be made clear and its soundness established; but how could that be? The overall accusation against all the Companions on account of this incident, which was from some of them at the beginning of their affair, and after which they performed countless acts of worship, is manifest folly and abundant ignorance.

*[Allusive interpretation]* (al-ishara) According to what has been said about the verses: ﴿It is He who raised among the unlettered a Messenger from among themselves, who recites to them His verses, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and the wisdom﴾ is an allusion to the greatness of His power, glory be to Him, and to the fact that the outpouring of knowledge does not depend on ordinary causes. From this, they said: the walī (saint, one who is close to Allah) may be unlettered, like the Shaykh Ma'ruf al-Karkhi, according to what Ibn al-Jawzi said, and he possesses *'ulum laduniyya* (knowledge bestowed directly by God) that intellects fall short of. And al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam said: A person may be knowing of Allah, the Exalted, and possess certainty, while not having knowledge of the *furud al-kifaya* (communal obligations). The Companions were more knowing than the scholars of the Successors (tabi'un) in the realities of certainty and the subtleties of gnosis, although some of the scholars among the Successors were more capable in *'ilm al-fiqh* (jurisprudence) than some of the Companions. Whoever devotes himself to Allah, the Exalted, and whose spirit becomes pure, divine lights are poured into his heart, by which he becomes prepared to perceive the divine sciences and the knowledge bestowed directly. Thus, sainthood certainly does not depend on knowing the formal sciences such as grammar, *ma'ani* (semantics), *bayan* (rhetoric), and other such disciplines, nor on knowing fiqh in its well-known form for instance. Rather, it depends on learning what a person is obligated to know of the *furud al-'ayn* (individual obligations), in whatever manner it is acquired, whether by reading, by hearing from a scholar, or the like. It is not conceivable for someone to be a saint who does not know what is incumbent upon him of the religious rulings, like most of those whose hands are kissed in our time. I have seen among them someone who, having reached about seventy years of age, when he recites the testimony, says "lā ilāha an-Allāh" in place of "lā ilāha illā Allāh." I said to him: "Since when have you been saying it this way?" He said: "Since my childhood until today." So I repeated the pure word to him, and he could not say it correctly except with effort. I do not think he would persist in that form. The report: "Allah does not take as a walī one who is ignorant; and if He took him, He would have made him knowing," is not from the words of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) (ﷺ), and even so, it does not benefit the claim of sainthood of those we have mentioned.

Some have mentioned that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and purifies them﴾ after His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿recites to them His verses﴾, is an allusion to the inner outpouring after the allusion to the outward verbal instruction. They said that this is achieved by the guiding saints, who purify their disciples (*murids*) by pouring lights into their hearts, until their hearts become pure and their souls grow pure. This is the secret of what is called *al-tawajjuh* (spiritual concentration) among the Naqshbandi masters. They also said: [it is achieved] through *al-rabita* (the spiritual bond), so that the heart may, through its blessing, become prepared for what is poured into it. I know of no reliable evidence for the establishment of this from the Greatest Lawgiver (ﷺ), nor from his Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them. Every proof they mention in this matter and regard as evidence is not free of a flaw; indeed, most of their arguments in it resemble grasping at the ropes of the moon. Were it not for fear of prolixity, I would have mentioned them along with their flaws. Nevertheless, I do not deny the blessing of each of the two matters, *al-tawajjuh* and *al-rabita*, and I have witnessed that by the grace of Allah, the Exalted.

Also, I do not claim with certainty that there is no evidence for it in reality, for over every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing. Perhaps the first of the masters who guided to these two practices found in them what is relied upon, or it may be said: what suffices for acting upon the like of this is something like what some of the eminent among their later ones relied upon, although there is room for discussion concerning it, and for its proponents there is a position regarding its matter.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and others﴾ etc., it is built upon its being conjoined to the pronoun in the accusative. It is said: it is an allusion to the non-cessation of his outpouring (ﷺ) upon his community until the Day of Resurrection. They have also said that the outpouring of the walī does not cease even after his transition from the abode of density and annihilation to the abode of detachment and permanence.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah﴾ etc., it is an allusion to the evil state of the deniers despite their knowledge. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: O you who have become Jews﴾ the verse, it is an allusion to the permissibility of testing one who claims sainthood, so that his condition may become manifest through the test; then at that point he is honored or humiliated. As for Allah's, the Exalted, reproach of those who withdrew, it is an allusion to a kind of method of training the disciple when some sort of deviation arises from him, so that he may follow the straight path and not commit transgression. And in the verses, beyond this, are allusions which the bounds of expressions cannot contain. "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah, the Exalted, will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he did not know."
